items.title: George Avakian interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 21, 1998
items.q: Condon again playing with Fats Waller on the famous five piece band session of 'Minor Drag'

ctx.x: When you say jazz has a foundation and a quality that doesn’t change, is it possible to put into words what that quality is?

Oh no, not really, and I’ll tell you it’s the old story of either Fats Waller or Louis Armstrong having told a lady, “Lady, if you don’t know what jazz is, you’ll never know” something like that. I asked both of them, did you really say that? And they laughed and said who knows? And Louis had one expression that he would use every now and then when someone asked him a question like that, which was, “Yeah, yeah, man, something like that.” Like the story of how scat singing began, when he dropped the music on the…

Yeah. That’s a good all-purpose term. And you were saying something yesterday I thought was really fascinating about how instrumentalists copied vocalists and how vocalists copied instrumentalists. And you had this kind of round about pattern.

items.title: Avakian George — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Fats Waller is mentioned only as a composer whose music Louis Armstrong recorded ('Fats having been a close friend of his') and as a contemporary artist on pickup dates ('like Billie Holiday and Fats Waller'). The interviewee (George Avakian) does not describe a personal interaction with Fats Waller

ctx.x: What was the most glorious moment musically?

There were certainly – maybe three. I’ll put it that way. One was absolutely listening to the Duke Ellington band at Newport playing Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue, which was a very surprise thing. I’ve written about it in the liner notes. So I’ll just say very briefly that this was not expected on the program. Duke threw it in at the last minute. Paul Gonsalves didn’t remember that he had played it once before, and he was of course the centerpiece of the whole thing. He blew into the wrong microphone, after I…

because apparently the band was pretty tight about the difficulty of the composition, which was not an easy composition. That’s when he said, “Let’s play something we haven’t played in a long time. Let’s play Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue.” That’s when Paul said, “But I don’t know the piece.” Duke said, “You’ve got the solo on this.” “What?” Yeah, “We’ll just bring you in for the key change, and I’ll take you out. That’s it. You just keep blowing the blues in between.” Another fantastic moment was after I had…
